\chapter{Taking Your Leave}
\label{ch:hi-taking-leave}
\hlchaptermodality{49}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say when I am leaving and when I will be back in Hindi.}

Complete HI-C49-meeting and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[abhī]{\hi{अभी} (abhī) — right now}

\label{lesson:HI-C49-now}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{śāyad} mean, and what did \emph{bilkul} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{अभी}}
\textbf{\hi{अभी}} (\emph{abhī}) — \textquotedblleft{}right now\textquotedblright{}.

\emph{Ab}, 'now', with the emphatic \emph{-hī} welded onto it: now and nothing but now. Behind \emph{ab} stands Sanskrit \emph{adhunā}.

That little \emph{-hī} is one of the most useful pieces in the language. It narrows whatever it lands on, and you will meet it stuck to other words later. Here it turns a vague present into a pointed one — not now-ish, but this moment, and no other.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five words for leaving.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{abhī}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{abhī}, then \emph{bilkul}, so the timing and the emphasis sit together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{अभी} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}right now\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[parsoṁ]{\hi{परसों} (parsoṁ) — the day after tomorrow}

\label{lesson:HI-C49-day-after}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{abhī} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{परसों}}
\textbf{\hi{परसों}} (\emph{parsoṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}the day after tomorrow\textquotedblright{}.

And also the day before yesterday. Like \hi{कल}, which does duty for both tomorrow and yesterday, \hi{परसों} counts two days out from today and leaves the direction to the sentence.

Sanskrit \emph{parasu}, 'the far day', lies underneath, and the language evidently never felt the lack of two separate words. Time is being measured here by distance from now, with the direction supplied by whatever the sentence is already doing.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two, and both of them are about when.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{parsoṁ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{parsoṁ}, then \emph{abhī}, the far day beside this very moment
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{परसों} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the day after tomorrow\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[safar]{\hi{सफ़र} (safar) — a journey}

\label{lesson:HI-C49-journey}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{parsoṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{सफ़र}}
\textbf{\hi{सफ़र}} (\emph{safar}) — \textquotedblleft{}a journey\textquotedblright{}.

Arabic \emph{safar}, 'travel', through Persian. The same root gives \emph{safīr}, an ambassador — somebody sent out on a journey and expected back.

The inherited word is \emph{yātrā}, from the Sanskrit root \emph{yā-}, 'to go', and it leans toward pilgrimage. So a \hi{सफ़र} is the road itself, while a \emph{yātrā} is the road with a reason at the end of it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three: right now, the far day, a journey.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{safar}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{safar}, then \emph{parsoṁ}, then \emph{abhī}, back down the run
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{सफ़र} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a journey\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nikalnā]{\hi{निकलना} (nikalnā) — to set out, to leave}

\label{lesson:HI-C49-set-out}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{safar} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{निकलना}}
\textbf{\hi{निकलना}} (\emph{nikalnā}) — \textquotedblleft{}to set out, to leave\textquotedblright{}.

What you say when you are on the point of walking out of a door. It is the going-out kind of action, where the thing leaves under its own steam, and it has a partner, \emph{nikālnā}, with a long \emph{ā}, which means to take something out.

Lengthen the vowel and the doer changes: that pairing is one of Hindi's tidiest machines, and it runs through dozens of everyday words. Sanskrit \emph{niṣkal-}, 'to go forth', stands behind both.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and this one is something you do.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nikalnā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{nikalnā}, then \emph{safar}, the leaving and the road it opens
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{निकलना} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}to set out, to leave\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mulāqāt]{\hi{मुलाक़ात} (mulāqāt) — a meeting}

\label{lesson:HI-C49-meeting}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{nikalnā} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{मुलाक़ात}}
\textbf{\hi{मुलाक़ात}} (\emph{mulāqāt}) — \textquotedblleft{}a meeting\textquotedblright{}.

Arabic \emph{mulāqāt}, on \emph{laqiya}, 'to meet', arriving through Persian. It covers everything from bumping into somebody on a street to a scheduled interview in an office.

It sits inside the ordinary parting line \emph{phir mulāqāt hogī}, 'there will be a meeting again' — which is what \hi{फिर} \hi{मिलेंगे} says using inherited material instead of borrowed. Same farewell, two vocabularies, and a speaker can pick either without changing the meaning by a hair.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five, and the run is closed: right now, the far day, a journey, setting out, a meeting.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mulāqāt}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{abhī}, \emph{parsoṁ}, \emph{safar}, \emph{nikalnā}, \emph{mulāqāt}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{मुलाक़ात} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a meeting\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
